# **Architectural Blueprint and Systems Analysis for SIH26176 — ORCA: Marine Ecosystem Reasoning with Collaborative Agents**

## **Executive Overview and Problem Statement Deconstruction**

Problem Statement \#20 (Portal ID: **SIH26176** / **26176**), titled *"ORCA: Marine EcOsystem Reasoning with Collaborative Agents,"* is a flagship software challenge issued by the **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)** / Department of Space for the Smart India Hackathon (SIH) 2026\. Within ISRO's 11-statement portfolio for the 2026 edition—which comprises 10 software challenges and 1 hardware challenge spanning lunar optical image correspondence (SIH26166) to onboard Bharatiya Antariksh Station (BAS) activity recognition (SIH26174)—ORCA serves as the primary operational bridge between spaceborne Earth Observation (EO) telemetry and grassroots maritime decision support. Across the broader SIH 2026 catalogue of 236 to 258 active problem statements and 84,127 submitted proposals (each competing for a ₹1,00,000 national award and ministry deployment mentorship), SIH26176 is cross-indexed across **Miscellaneous**, **Space Technology**, **Disaster Management**, and **Geospatial AI** tracks.  
The core challenge addressed by ORCA stems from an acute structural asymmetry in India's blue economy. Every day, ISRO and partner global oceanographic agencies generate vast volumes of satellite Earth Observation and in-situ marine telemetry, including Sea Surface Temperature (SST), chlorophyll-a (Chl\\text{-}a) concentration, ocean surface wind vectors, wave height spectra, and weather forecasts. Marine stakeholders—including coastal and deep-sea fishermen, marine researchers, coastal authorities, and disaster management agencies—depend on these variables to safeguard lives, support food security, protect biodiversity, optimize maritime transportation, and maintain coastal resilience. However, these datasets remain siloed across heterogeneous scientific portals (such as ISRO's MOSDAC, NRSC's Bhoonidhi, and MoES-INCOIS bulletins) in complex raster formats (NetCDF, HDF5, GeoTIFF) that require specialized GIS processing to interpret.  
To resolve this operational bottleneck, ISRO's specification mandates an **Agentic AI-powered Marine Intelligence Platform** capable of interpreting plain-language queries, autonomously discovering, retrieving, and integrating relevant satellite, marine, meteorological, and geospatial datasets, performing spatial, temporal, and contextual correlation across heterogeneous sources, and delivering explainable, evidence-backed advisories through conversational responses, maps, alerts, and interactive geospatial visualizations. Rather than functioning as a simple retrieval wrapper over individual datasets, the platform must execute autonomous planning, tool selection, task decomposition, multi-turn contextual dialogue, and automatic language identification with native response generation across Indian regional languages.

A rigorous examination of these competitive metrics reveals a central engineering paradox. On the surface, SIH26176 exhibits high specification clarity (4/5) and straightforward demonstrability, as a plain-language query asking whether it is safe to fish tomorrow morning immediately resonates with evaluators. Consequently, the problem statement attracted 412 idea submissions out of the 500-submission cap prior to portal closure. However, its acceptance potential, feasibility, and architectural novelty are constrained at 3/5, while required build effort is classified as *Massive*.  
This divergence occurs because generic multi-agent orchestration using off-the-shelf frameworks (such as LangGraph or CrewAI) has become a commoditized design pattern in 2026\. In a safety-critical maritime environment, a conversational platform that generates fluent vernacular text but hallucinates wave heights, miscalculates International Maritime Boundary Line (IMBL) distances, or masks stale satellite feeds behind complex agent choreography poses severe real-world hazards to human life and vessel security. For an ISRO evaluation panel, competitive differentiation lies entirely in **oceanographic physics grounding, deterministic safety guardrails, and verifiable source provenance** rather than conversational polish.

## **Oceanographic Telemetry and Satellite Earth Observation Grounding**

A foundational requirement of SIH26176 is the integration of authentic Indian spaceborne and oceanographic data streams, primarily sourced from ISRO's **Meteorological and Oceanographic Satellite Data Archival Centre (MOSDAC)**, the **National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) Bhoonidhi** portal, and the **Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS)**. Engineering an operational ingestion pipeline requires navigating concrete sensor constraints, orbital duty cycles, and hardware realities that distinguish domain-accurate architectures from superficial prototypes.

### **Spaceborne Sensor Architecture and the EOS-06 SSTM Hardware Reality**

ISRO's primary polar-orbiting ocean observation asset is **EOS-06 (Oceansat-3)**, a 1,117 kg third-generation spacecraft launched on November 26, 2022 aboard PSLV-C54 into a sun-synchronous orbit to maintain continuity with Oceansat-1 (1999), Oceansat-2 (2009), and SCATSAT-1 (2016). EOS-06 was designed to simultaneously capture biological, physical, and atmospheric oceanic parameters via four payloads: the 13-band Ocean Colour Monitor (**OCM-3**), the Ku-band Scatterometer (**SCAT-3**), the 2-band Sea Surface Temperature Monitor (**SSTM**), and the French CNES **ARGOS** data collection platform.  
An essential technical nuance documented by ISRO's Space Applications Centre (SAC) and MOSDAC is that **the SSTM payload onboard EOS-06 developed a mechanical scan anomaly post-launch and is currently non-operational**. While SSTM was engineered with two split-window thermal infrared channels—TIR1 (10.75\\text{--}11.25\\ \\mu\\text{m}) and TIR2 (11.75\\text{--}12.25\\ \\mu\\text{m})—to deliver 1 km global SST rasters, any SIH26176 architecture claiming to ingest live SST directly from EOS-06 SSTM exposes a critical gap in domain verification. To achieve operational SST grounding until the deployment of **Oceansat-3A** (which carries replacement SSTM-1, OCM-3, SCAT-3, and MATHS payloads), the ingestion pipeline must fuse EOS-06's active OCM-3 and SCAT-3 feeds with thermal infrared SST products from ISRO's geostationary **INSAT-3D and INSAT-3DS** meteorological payloads (positioned at 82°E with an 18-band Advanced Imager providing 500 m visible and 2 km IR resolution, plus a dedicated Lightning Mapper) alongside polar-orbiting **MODIS/VIIRS** (1 km) and **Copernicus Marine / NOAA ERDDAP** datasets.

### **Algorithmic Mechanics of Potential Fishing Zone (PFZ) Delimitation**

In the Indian Ocean—spanning the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal (5°N–23°N, 78°E–95°E)—pelagic and demersal fish stocks do not distribute uniformly; they aggregate along dynamic hydrographic discontinuities known as **thermal and biophysical fronts**. When nutrient-rich, cooler subsurface water upwells or collides with warmer surface water masses, phytoplankton blooms proliferate (indicated by elevated Chl\\text{-}a and Fluorescence Line Height measured by OCM-3's 13 narrow bands), attracting zooplankton and schooling pelagic predators such as sardines, mackerel, anchovies, and tuna.  
To move beyond static text scraping of published bulletins, an advanced ORCA PFZ Agent executes a four-stage geophysical computation pipeline grounded in validated Indian oceanographic literature. In the first stage, rather than relying solely on naive spatial gradient filters that amplify sensor noise, operational PFZ systems utilize the **Cayula-Cornillon (1992) single-image edge detection algorithm** supplemented by the **Canny (1986) detector**. The algorithm passes a 32 \\times 32 pixel moving window at a stride of 16 pixels across the satellite SST raster. Within each window, pixel temperatures are tested for statistical **bimodality**, which indicates the presence of two distinct water masses. If a bimodal distribution is confirmed, the absolute difference between the mean temperatures of the two populations (\\Delta \\mu \= \\vert{}\\mu\_1 \- \\mu\_2\\vert{}) is evaluated against stepped thermal front thresholds of 0.3^\\circ\\text{C}, 0.4^\\ci\[span\_269\](start\_span)\[span\_269\](end\_span)rc\\text{C}, and 0.5^\\circ\\text{C}. Windows exceeding the threshold delineate active thermal fronts, outperforming older single-gradient approaches.  
In the second stage, the agent computes the biophysical gradient magnitude coupling across co-registered SST and Chl\\text{-}a grids:  
I\_{\\text{PFZ}}(x,y) \= \\vert{}\\nabla \\text{SST}(x,y)\\vert{} \\times \\vert{}\\nabla \\text{Chl-}a(x,y)\\vert{}  
where \\nabla f \= \\left(\\frac{\\partial f}{\\partial x}, \\frac{\\partial f}{\\partial y}\\right) represents the spatial rate of change. High values of I\_{\\text{PFZ}} co-located with Chl\\text{-}a \> 0.1\\ \\text{mg/m}^3 and cold-core cyclonic eddies—detected via satellite altimetry down to a 400\\ \\text{km} horizontal scale and 5\\ \\text{cm} amplitude, where upward Ekman transport injects nutrients into the euphotic zone—signify prime pelagic foraging habitats.  
The third stage addresses a major operational vulnerability of optical ocean color sensors (OCM-3, MODIS) and thermal IR radiometers: severe data loss under cloud cover, particularly during the Southwest and Northeast monsoons. To maintain continuous advisory coverage during cloudy periods, the PFZ pipeline computes **3-day rolling averages** of Chl\\text{-}a and tracks **thermal front persistence** across 7 consecutive days by generating a 5\\ \\text{km} spatial buffer around day t\_0 fronts and incrementing a persistence counter (+1 per day) wherever subsequent daily fronts intersect the buffer. When optical imagery is obscured on day t, persistent fronts from day t-1 are mathematically advected forward using the **relative wind vector** (\\vec{V}\_{\\text{rel}}) derived from cloud-penetrating microwave scatterometer (EOS-06 SCAT-3) winds and surface current vectors:  
\\vec{V}\_{\\text{rel}} \= \\vec{V}\_{\\text{wind}} \- \\vec{V}\_{\\text{current}}  
In the fourth stage, candidate zones are classified into three deterministic confidence tiers based on multi-parameter Bay of Bengal validation frameworks: **Lower Possibility** (presence of any 1 feature among high Chl\\text{-}a, thermal front, or cyclonic eddy), **Medium Possibility** (co-location of any 2 features), and **Higher Possibility** (co-location of all 3 features: Chl\\text{-}\[span\_139\](start\_span)\[span\_139\](end\_span)\[span\_144\](start\_span)\[span\_144\](end\_span)a \> 0.1\\ \\text{mg/m}^3, active thermal front, and cyclonic cold-core eddy). Empirical field validations conducted by the Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute (CMFRI), Fishery Survey of India (FSI), Space Applications Centre (SAC), and INCOIS along the Kerala coast—which spans 590\\ \\text{km}, contributes over 6 lakh metric tonnes to India's 32 lakh metric tonne annual marine production, and serves roughly 30,000 PFZ user boat owners (30% of the fleet)—demonstrate the transformative economic value of this pipeline. Simultaneous ring-seine (Thanguvala and Chooda vala) and gillnet validation operations confirm that vessels utilizing satellite PFZ advisories achieve an average catch revenue of ₹81,000 (at ₹45/kg against ₹46,100 operating expenditure, yielding ₹34,900 net profit) compared to ₹31,500 revenue (against ₹21,700 expenditure, yielding ₹9,800 net profit) for non-PFZ operations—representing a **256% increase in net operational profit** alongside substantial reductions in scouting time and fuel consumption.

## **Collaborative Multi-Agent Topology and Deterministic Safety Guardrails**

While the problem statement emphasizes collaborative AI agents, empirical systems literature demonstrates that naive multi-agent LLM architectures suffer from three critical failure modes in scientific and engineering domains: **hallucination in the absence of structured knowledge graphs or taxonomies**, **substantial errors on complex mathematical calculations**, and **context-window saturation** when raw telemetry dumps are concatenated across agents.

### **Neuro-Symbolic Division of Labor: Planner-Guided Layered Execution Graphs**

To eliminate these failure modes, a production-grade ORCA platform must enforce a strict neuro-symbolic architectural boundary: **deterministic geophysical and maritime rules compute the safety state and spatial coordinates, while the Large Language Model orchestrates task routing, cross-source correlation, and natural-language explanation**.  
Recent empirical evaluations of multi-agent hydrodynamic decision systems (*Towards Multi-Agent Autonomous Reasoning in Hydrodynamics*, arXiv:2605.01102v1) establish the optimal topology for this workload: a **Planner-Guided Layered Execution Graph (LEG)**—a dynamically constructed Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) backed by an allowlisted agent registry and **Ocean MCP (Model Context Protocol)** tool servers. Rather than forcing every user query through a rigid, monolithic sequence, the runtime separates agents into **General-Purpose Control Agents** (such as the Graph Architect, Consolidator, Cross-Track Merge, Image Interpreter, and Reporter) and **Domain Specialist Agents**.

### **Empirical Validation of Dynamic Graph Planning and Context Compaction**

The architectural necessity of dynamic graph construction and intermediate consolidation is proven by controlled ablation experiments on hydrodynamic multi-agent systems. When the dynamic *Graph Architect* is replaced by a **Fixed Graph** pipeline that routes every query through an identical static sequence of specialists (\[NHC\] \-\> \[NOAA CO-OPS, USGS\] \-\> \[FEMA\]), **Factual Precision plummets by 28.7 percentage points**, **Topology Selection drops by 28.6 percentage points**, and **Agent F1 falls by 20.1 percentage points**. Static pipelines fail because they cannot decompose multi-part maritime queries into isolated parallel tracks, forcing downstream agents to juggle disparate data simultaneously while irrelevant specialists dilute the context available to the Reporter.  
Conversely, when the **Consolidator** is disabled (**No Consolidation** ablation, where per-layer and cross-track context compaction is replaced with raw text concatenation), **Factual Precision drops by 4.6 percentage points**, confirming that structured intermediate merging genuinely assists the Reporter in extracting accurate numerical values from multi-source telemetry. Remarkably, however, **Source Attribution increases by 8.9 percentage points** under the *No Consolidation* condition because unfiltered specialist tool outputs contain dense technical tokens—such as exact station IDs, vertical datums, and UTC timestamps—that a condensed natural-language brief strips out.  
To capture the \+4.6 percentage point precision gain of consolidation *without* suffering the 8.9 percentage point loss in provenance tokens, best-in-class SIH26176 implementations (such as orca-sih26176 and orca-marine-assistant) decouple provenance metadata from LLM text summarization. Provenance tokens are written directly by the deterministic tool wrappers into a structured **Evidence Ledger** side-channel, guaranteeing 100% citation fidelity alongside concise natural-language synthesis.

### **Hard Safety Guardrails, Strict Abstention, and Honest Fallback Protocols**

Because coastal departure advisories carry immediate life-safety consequences, leading ORCA implementations enforce three non-negotiable deterministic guardrails across all execution paths. First, the language model is strictly prohibited from computing or altering the safety state. Instead, a deterministic risk calculator ingests validated numerical telemetry (wind speed, significant wave height, swell period, cyclone proximity, and lightning density) and computes a bounded **Fishermen Sea-Venture Safety Index** (0\\text{--}100) equipped with hard safety floors, where any single extreme hazard immediately forces an EXTREME no-go state regardless of benign averages. In the reference orca-sih26176 benchmark suite, five rehearsed scenarios (/?demo=safe|danger|cyclone|pfz|route) lock verifiable baseline verdicts across distinct Indian maritime regimes: **Goa** evaluates to a score of **9 (LOW risk)** suitable for departure; **Mumbai at 06:00 IST** evaluates to **70 (HIGH risk)** due to morning wind-wave shear; and **Paradip (Odisha)** under cyclonic swell evaluates to **92 (EXTREME risk)**.  
Second, as implemented by Team SagarMitra (138259), if an upstream telemetry feed is unreachable, corrupted, or lacks spatial coverage for the queried coordinates, the safety engine triggers a **Strict Abstention Protocol**. Rather than allowing the LLM to extrapolate or fabricate plausible weather conditions, the system returns an explicit "UNKNOWN" safety verdict and halts advisory generation. Third, because live government oceanographic feeds frequently experience latency or maintenance downtime, architectures such as orca-marine-assistant (tarang-shah-18) and Team OrbitX's prototype wrap Open-Meteo, GDACS, and Indian satellite feeds in a Time-To-Live (TTL) cache equipped with per-product freshness flags. If a live endpoint times out, the system transitions into an **Honest Reference Fallback** mode: it serves the last verified snapshot or rehearsed reference baseline while prominently stamping the UI with the exact data age, provider availability status, and the mandatory legal boundary stating that the output is *"decision support, not an official advisory"* and never replaces official IMD or INCOIS bulletins.

|  | **ORCA Decision Intelligence** *(Team OrbitX)* & **FisherNav** *(Slayy Stack)* | Deterministic rule separation (OrbitX) and offline edge navigation for deep-sea return (FisherNav). | Multi-agent system with **EdgeAI** and offline navigation caching. | MOSDAC / PFZ integration with explicit disclosure of data freshness and provider limitations. |

### **Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) and Visual Ergonomics for Maritime Environments**

A profound design divergence separates winning maritime decision support systems from conventional hackathon dashboards. Most software teams default to dark-mode neon interfaces that mimic sci-fi command centers. However, as demonstrated in the design engineering of orca-sih26176, dark dashboards fail both in the field—under high-glare tropical sunlight on a wet boat deck—and in the evaluation room, where dark interfaces wash out on standard conference projectors. Anchoring the visual identity in the **visual language of drafted nautical sea charts** immediately establishes cognitive trust among fishers, harbour pilots, and port officers who already read hydrographic charts.

| Design System Dimension | Token / Scale Specification | Hex / Numeric Values | Functional & Ergonomic Mandate |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Chart Paper Surfaces (70% Area)** | paper-50 / paper-100 / paper-150..400 | \#FBF7ED / \#F5EEDD / \#EFE6CF..\#B9A67C | High-luminance drafted sheet background for outdoor sunlight legibility and projector clarity. |
| **Hydrographic Inks (25% Area)** | ink-900 / ink-800..700 / ink-500..400 / ink-300 | \#12212D / \#1B2F3E..\#263B4D / \#42596D..\#5A6F81 / \#82949F | ink-400 (\#5A6F81) is the lightest permitted text ink (4.51:1 contrast on \#F5EE\[span\_456\](start\_span)\[span\_456\](end\_span)DD); ink-300 is restricted to non-text decoration. |
| **Chart & Signal Accents** | chart-500 / sea / signal | \#2A7391 / \#CFE0E6 / \#C7442E | Focus rings, interactive links, sea tile background, and buoy-red restricted no-go marks. |
| **Semantic Risk Tokens (Status Only)** | risk-low / risk-moderate / risk-high / risk-extreme | \#1D7A50 / \#A17000 / \#BF4E12 / \#AF2318 | Strictly reserved for safety verdicts and ground ratings; never used for decorative UI chrome. |
| **SST & Fish Chance Scales** | sst-cold..hot / chance-good..poor | \#3E7A99..\#BF6A1F / \#63862B..\#9C5F44 | Continuous thermal contour shading and fishing ground likelihood tiers below risk-low. |
| **Self-Hosted Variable Typography** | Fraunces \+ Noto Serif Devanagari / Archivo / Spline Sans Mono | 9-step minor-third (1.2\\times) scale (11px to 48px) | Bundled via @fontsource-variable with zero external CDN dependencies; 11px floor enforced on all informative labels. |

Beyond color and typographic discipline, maritime ergonomics requires fail-safe DOM rendering and dual-persona synchronization. Because low-end smartphones used by coastal fishers at 4:00 AM may drop frames or fail to execute WebGL/Canvas particle animations, safety-critical metrics—the 0–100 risk dial (40px), departure window, return-by timestamp (28px), and rubber-stamp verdict—are rendered immediately in the static DOM and never hidden behind an animation gate that might fail to execute. Simultaneously, the platform synchronizes its **Fisher Phone View** (which prioritizes a prominent LISTEN TTS audio briefing in the user's regional language for low-literacy accessibility) with a **District Authority Board** (33px display totals) that scores every landing centre along the coast using the exact same underlying Evidence Ledger—preventing conflicting actions between grassroots boat operators and harbour master control rooms.

## **Strategic Conclusions and Production Engineering Recommendations**

Synthesizing the official ISRO problem specification, oceanographic remote sensing constraints, and empirical multi-agent systems benchmarks yields a cohesive production blueprint for building a jury-winning and field-deployable ORCA platform. First and foremost, system architects must enforce a strict neuro-symbolic firewall around all maritime safety verdicts. A generative language model must never be permitted to directly output a go/no-go sea-venture recommendation or extrapolate missing meteorological values. Instead, a deterministic rule engine with hard safety floors must compute the 0–100 Sea-Venture Safety Index, backed by a Strict Abstention Protocol that outputs an explicit UNKNOWN state when live telemetry is unavailable and an Honest Reference Fallback that transparently flags cached or simulated data.  
Second, the data ingestion layer must explicitly account for the **EOS-06 SSTM hardware anomaly** through multi-mission sensor fusion. Both the architectural documentation and the runtime Evidence Ledger should reflect that while EOS-06 (Oceansat-3) provides operational 13-band OCM-3 chlorophyll (366\\ \\text{m}) and SCAT-3 Ku-band wind and coastal upwelling (25\\ \\text{km}) products via MOSDAC and Bhoonidhi, its onboard SSTM sensor is currently inactive due to a scan mechanism fault. Operational thermal infrared SST must therefore be ingested from **INSAT-3D/3DS**, **MODIS/VIIRS**, or **Oceansat-3A**, while SCAT-3 relative wind vectors (\\vec{V}\_{\\text{wind}} \- \\vec{V}\_{\\text{current}\[span\_106\](start\_span)\[span\_106\](end\_span)\[span\_112\](start\_span)\[span\_112\](end\_span)}) and 7-day buffer persistence are utilized to advect Cayula-Cornillon bimodal thermal fronts across monsoon cloud gaps.  
Third, the multi-agent orchestration layer should adopt a **Planner-Guided Layered Execution Graph (LEG)** paired with side-channel provenance tracking. Replacing static agent chains with a dynamic Graph Architect that selects allowlisted specialists per query captures a documented \+28.7 percentage point gain in factual precision, while pairing a Consolidator node with an out-of-band Evidence Ledger preserves raw provenance tokens—such as buoy station IDs, satellite pass UTC timestamps, spatial resolutions, and confidence tiers—without saturating the LLM context window.  
Finally, to deliver comprehensive coast-wide utility, the platform must integrate sovereign maritime geofencing, weather-aware pathfinding, and keyless offline reproducibility. Coupling an **IMBL Geofencing Agent** (monitoring real-time vector distances to the India-Sri Lanka, India-Pakistan, and India-Bangladesh maritime borders) with an **A^\* Vessel Route Optimizer** enables the system to plot fuel-optimized waypoints around hatched high-wave polygons and restricted border buffers, directly resolving queries \#6 and \#8 of the official specification. Packaging this pipeline with a one-click local launcher (DEMO mode pre-loaded with validated coastal scenarios across Goa, Mumbai, and Paradip alongside LIVE Open-Meteo, GDACS, and Ocean MCP connectors), a high-contrast drafted sea-chart interface, and bidirectional voice dialogue across 8 to 11 Indian coastal languages ensures that ORCA functions as a trustworthy, life-saving instrument for India's maritime communities.
